title: A flat module with complete devissage becomes projective after base localization
statement: Let $R\to S$ be a homomorphism of commutative rings of finite presentation [def-weil-pbc-finitely-presented-algebra], let $N$ be a finitely presented $S$-module [def-sc-finitely-presented-module] which is flat as an $R$-module [def-weil-pbc-flat-ring-map], and let $\mathfrak r\subset R$ be a prime ideal. If $N/S/R$ admits a complete dévissage over $\mathfrak r$ [def-trf-complete-algebra-devissage], then there exists $f\in R\setminus\mathfrak r$ such that $N_f=N\otimes_RR_f$ is a projective $R_f$-module [def-weil-pbc-projective-module]. Here $R_f$ is the ring obtained by inverting $1,f,f^2,\ldots$, and $N_f$ is equivalently the module of fractions $m/f^k$. No finite generation or finite presentation of $N$ as an $R$-module is assumed.

proof.text: Induct on the length $n$ of the given complete dévissage. The inductive claim at length $n$ is the statement of this lemma for every commutative ring $R$, every prime $\mathfrak r\subset R$, every finitely presented $R$-algebra $S$ and every finitely presented $S$-module $N$ flat over $R$ admitting a complete dévissage over $\mathfrak r$ of length $n$; the base ring is quantified because step 5 replaces $R$ by a localization $R_{f_1}$ before the hypothesis is applied in step 7. At length zero the definition requires $N=0$; take $f=1$, since the zero module has the lifting property for projectivity. At positive length write the data as $(A_i,B_i,M_i,\alpha_i)_{1\leq i\leq n}$, with $\alpha_i:B_i^{\oplus r_i}\to M_i$. The isomorphism $N\cong M_1$ is $R$-linear, so $M_1$ is $R$-flat, and it suffices to establish projectivity for a localization of $M_1$.

For each $i$, the affine morphism $\operatorname{Spec}B_i\to\operatorname{Spec}R$ is smooth. The affine smoothness equivalence gives a smooth ring map $R\to B_i$, hence a finitely presented algebra by the definition of smooth ring map, and a flat module by smooth-flatness. Smoothness also gives geometrically reduced fibres. Together with the geometrically irreducible fibres in the dévissage this gives geometrically integral fibres: after any residue-field extension the fibre is nonempty, reduced and irreducible, hence integral. Thus each $R\to B_i$ satisfies the ring hypotheses of the generic-basis shrinking lemma and the projectivity theorem for geometrically integral fibres.

The surjective finitely presented map $S\to A_1$ is finite (the element $1$ generates $A_1$ as an $S$-module). The finite-extension presentation theorem therefore makes $M_1$ finitely presented over $A_1$. Composition makes $A_1$ finitely presented over $R$. Also $B_1\to A_1$ is finitely presented: choose finite presentations $A_1=R[x]/(F)$ and $B_1=R[y]/(G)$ and polynomials $P_j(x)$ representing the images of $y_j$. Then $A_1=B_1[x]/(F,y_j-P_j(x))$, since eliminating the $y_j$ leaves exactly $R[x]/(F)$; the relations $G(P(x))$ already vanish there. This is a finite presentation over $B_1$. As $B_1\to A_1$ is finite by the dévissage, the same finite-extension theorem now makes $M_1$ finitely presented over $B_1$.

proof.text: Apply the generic-basis shrinking lemma to $R\to B_1$, $M_1$, and the given $\alpha_1$. Its generic-fibre isomorphism is one of the dévissage conditions. The ideal $\mathfrak p_1=\mathfrak rB_1$ is prime by that definition, and contracts to $\mathfrak r$: the nonzero fibre algebra has an injective structure map from the field $\kappa(\mathfrak r)$, so a scalar outside $\mathfrak r$ cannot belong to $\mathfrak rB_1$. All finite-presentation and flatness hypotheses were verified in the preceding steps. Obtain $f_1\notin\mathfrak r$ for which $(\alpha_1)_{f_1}$ is universally injective over $R_{f_1}$.

Localize the entire diagram at $f_1$ and write $R\leftarrow R_{f_1}$, with the analogous replacements of its algebras and modules, and $\mathfrak r\leftarrow\mathfrak rR_{f_1}$. The dévissage conditions persist. Smoothness persists by base change; the fibres over primes of $R_{f_1}$ are the original fibres at the corresponding primes of $R$, so their geometric irreducibility persists. Finite spanning sets still span finite algebras, and algebra presentations remain finite by base change. Localization preserves exactness: a fraction in a kernel is represented by an element whose image is killed by a power of $f_1$, which can be multiplied into its numerator. Hence cokernels, surjections and the specified isomorphisms localize. The residue-field condition is unchanged because $f_1\notin\mathfrak r$. A finite presentation matrix localizes to a finite presentation matrix; flatness of $M_1$ over the localized base follows from $L\otimes_{R_{f_1}}(M_1)_{f_1}\cong L\otimes_R M_1$ for an $R_{f_1}$-module $L$. We may therefore continue with $\alpha_1$ universally injective over the current base.

Set $C=\operatorname{coker}(\alpha_1)$ over the current rings. Universal injectivity and the quotient description of $C$ give a universally exact sequence $0\to B_1^{\oplus r_1}\xrightarrow{\alpha_1}M_1\to C\to0$. Indeed tensoring a cokernel is again the cokernel, and the initial map is injective by the meaning of universal injectivity. The flat-cokernel theorem now gives that $C$ is $R$-flat. Moreover $C$ is finitely presented over $B_1$: choose a presentation $B_1^u\to B_1^v\to M_1\to0$ and lift the images of the $r_1$ standard basis vectors under $\alpha_1$ to $B_1^v$; append those $r_1$ columns to the presentation matrix. The resulting matrix $B_1^{u+r_1}\to B_1^v$ presents $C$. If $n=1$, then $C=0$. If $n>1$, the identifications $C\cong M_2$ and $\operatorname{coker}\alpha_i\cong M_{i+1}$ exhibit the tail $(A_i,B_i,M_i,\alpha_i)_{2\leq i\leq n}$ as a complete dévissage of $C/B_1/R$ of length $n-1$.

When $n>1$, apply the induction hypothesis to $C/B_1/R$. The base algebra $B_1$ is finitely presented over $R$ by step 2; $C$ is finitely presented over $B_1$ and flat over $R$ by step 6, and the required tail dévissage has just been specified. It gives $h\in R\setminus\mathfrak r$ such that $C_h$ is projective over $R_h$. When $n=1$, take $h=1$ and $C_h=0$, which is projective. The universal-injective sequence of step 6 stays exact after this further localization by the fraction argument of step 5.

The algebra $(B_1)_h$ over the current $R_h$ is flat and finitely presented and has geometrically integral fibres, by step 2 and the localization checks of step 5. The projectivity theorem for flat finitely presented algebras with geometrically integral fibres gives that $(B_1)_h$ is a projective $R_h$-module. A finite direct sum of projective modules is projective: lift a map from each summand along a surjection and add the finitely many lifts. Thus $(B_1)_h^{\oplus r_1}$ is projective, also when $r_1=0$.

Projectivity of $C_h$ lifts $\mathrm{id}_{C_h}$ along the quotient $q:(M_1)_h	woheadrightarrow C_h$, giving a section $s$. The map $(b,c)\mapsto(\alpha_1)_h(b)+s(c)$ identifies $(B_1)_h^{\oplus r_1}\oplus C_h$ with $(M_1)_h$: subtract $s(q(m))$ from $m$ to obtain the unique element of the kernel. Hence $(M_1)_h$, and therefore the corresponding localization of $N$, is projective by the same finite-sum lifting argument. To express the successive restrictions by one element of the original $R$, write $h=a/f_1^k$ in $R_{f_1}$. Since $h

The fraction maps $m/(f_1^i h^j)\mapsto f_1^{kj}m/(f_1^i a^j)$ identify the corresponding module localizations. This gives the asserted projective $R_f$-module $N_f$.
